projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Bellock was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Today is October 6. I am Kristina Kalchev and I am interviewing (interviewee's name John Bellock at (address) 3685 Vista Campana North Ocean Side, CA 92057. (State relationship to interviewee) Mr. Bellock is a family friend. Mr. Bellock is 87 years old and was born on Jan 7, 1920. Mr. Bellock served in (war) WWII, Korea. Mr. Bellock was in (unit) many engineering units and held the following rank: seaman to chief petty officer.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Where did you live prior to serving?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: North Dakota, on a farm in North Dakota.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: How was life like in North Dakota compared to your years of service?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Very poor. It was daylight to dark it, was hard labor, it was rough living.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Were you drafted into the military and if not explain why you chose the navy?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No. Well, very early in my life I saw one of the men that lived around there come home and he was in Navy uniform and that was it. I never saw a body of water that I couldn't look across but I chose the Navy and that's it.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What about that man intrigued you to join the navy?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: When did he join?

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: No, what about the man that you saw in uniform, what about him made you want to join?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: I didn't understand the last of that question.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What about the man, why did he make you want to join the navy, what intrigued you?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Just to see him in uniform.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Yeah, just the professionalism of it?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Yeah, just because he was in Navy uniform.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What were your first days of service like or what happened once you signed up? And what emotions did you feel during that time?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well, I signed up in Minneapolis, Minnesota and went to Great Lakes Naval training center, at boot camp they call it. Is that what you mean boot camp?

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Yeah, what happened once you signed up until you got on a ship and were sent off pretty much?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: After boot camp we were, - Instead of twelve weeks they broke us at ten weeks because they needed the sailors on ships because Hitler had already been moving on 1 September 1939. This was 1939 when this happened. They sent two companies, companies fifteen and sixteen and we all went board the USS Texas, a battleship.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What emotions were you feeling at the time? Were you scared, were you anxious, were you excited, what?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, there was no time I was scared, just everything was new to me.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: So it was more of an experience more of like a new [?]

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Oh, I had no experience what so ever.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: So what was living on a ship like? Was there any good memories, I mean what did you eat; give me kind of a day-to-day thing that happened on a ship.

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well, I really don't know what the food was, but I was assigned to the - When we lined up on Monday morning, the first Monday morning there, we had an officer walk down the ranks and he said, "Hey You!" I was one of his "Hey You's" that he pulled out of ranks and he took three of us down below and he asked me what I'd want, the ice machines, the evaporators, or the machine shop. Well, I guess I was thinking of my stomach because ice machine is refrigeration and that's where they keep food.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What did you do pretty much on the ship when you weren't training or whatever?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well, because we were the lowest on the totem pole we scrubbed paintwork and shined the steel deck and took lessons on how to start a compressor, a CO2 compressor, carbon dioxide.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What rank were you considered? You were sailor right?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Engineering.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What was your top service rank that you ever got?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Chief Petty Officer, CPO. Chief Machinist Mate.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: So describe the sequence of events when your Naval plane took over a ship and what was the name of that ship and why did you have to take it over?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Oh, down in the Caribbean?

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Yes, when you took over .

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: You're going to have to take a minute here until I got this thing out here to look. You want the name of them?

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Yes, the name of the ships and the sequence of events and why you were taking them over.

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: The ship I was on at the time was the USS Goldsborough, it was AVD number 5, it was a seaplane tender, (PBY's); - they landed on and took off from water. And we were tied up to the fruit docks in Honduras. I was on the docks at the time when they passed the word they call away to what is referred to as the boarding party. In other words we leave our ship and go aboard any ship we are taking over as boarding. Anyway, they flew us out there on two PBY's and eleven unlisted men, which I was one, and two officers. We landed out there and went aboard this one ship and where is it [?]

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: When you patrol plane landed, what happened from the moment you landed to taking over the ship?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well, we went aboard we pulled out their flag and ran up the American flag, the Stars and Stripes. And we took the ship in the Belize, British Honduras. Belize, British Honduras was under British flag at the time and we took it over and turned it over to the British authorities and then we checked for contraband on board as to what they were possibly hauling to help the German submarines. And they found out in their logs that they carried numerous drums of diesel oil. They would rendezvous with the German submarines and furnish them food and diesel oil and supplies.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Who was running these ships? Who was in control like what country or what group?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Gough, [from article] "the plot thickens in march when one of these ships spotted running at full speed with a deck load of oil drums, suspicion turned on Gough".

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What affiliation or country was Gough with?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: He was just a native down there, he worked out of Panama.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: So he was a person?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Yes, [reads excerpt from article]

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: So how did you take over the ship? When you landed what happened?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well, a PBY was flying around them with a .50 caliber trained on them with a stock out there and when our PBY landed, we took our rubber boats and rowed over to them and went aboard and took over.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: How exactly did you take over? Did you take over by killing everyone?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, we knew what we had to do, they took it out I don't know how many miles in Belize and that was it. Three days later they found another ship out there and they flew us back out and we brought that ship in.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: So the crewmembers of the ships that you took over were then held prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Were you ever injured in these raids?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, let me take a step further. On the second ship we picked up this Gough, this guy in charge of all of it, he had his wife and two kids, so we caught the guy and then we took him back to Belize and the British took him. By word of mouth, I can't prove it, but he was supposedly shot in Jamaica.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Was the Nazi's paying him to do this?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Oh yes, before the war they set it up. Many years before they all set this up where they all rendezvous at the different islands down there. The Pirate Blue Beard [?] back in some of the coves where he used to anchor in there when he was a pirate and used to go out and capture ships, they used those coves.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Can you give me a little bit more detail on how you captured these ships?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well, we just went aboard, another man and I were the engineers in this crew and he and I went down in the engine room. The other crew with their side arms on, the 45's, went up to He Bridge and took over there and that's it. They didn't stop us at all, we didn't have any trouble with the crew.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: There wasn't any casualties?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, none what so ever.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: And you were never scared at any of this time at all?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: How did you contact or stay in touch with your family throughout your service? Was it hard to be away from them?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, not really. They forced us to write letters when we were in boot training but when we left boot training we were on our own. Very little correspondence back and forth with my family.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies when you were on your voyages?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Yes, we always had food on board ship. There was no mal-nutrition in the Navy, it wasn't the best food, but there was no mal-nutrition.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: When you were in the Bahamas, Equator area, what areas were you in exactly throughout your voyages?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: St. Lucia is one, Aruba, Jamaica, Reciefe, Brazil, Panama (both coasts), Galapagos Islands. We set up station to service a PBY at all those places.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: When you were at all those places what did you think of the officers or did you make friends with soldiers or other Navy crew?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, not really. No we were pretty well restricted aboard ship and we were off by ourselves on these coves so we were far from towns and what not. We just had our own ship and that was it. We did our job right there.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Did you ever take pictures or document what happened in a dairy?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No cameras allowed and we could not keep a diary because in case we were captured and the enemy took over, they would know what we were doing.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What did you do to entertain yourself?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Not a heck of a lot. We had one movie that they'd bring in and we would show it about three or four times a week. Just for the heck of it the movie operator ran the film backwards for a while.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What were your feelings when your service ended because I know afterward you continued working for the Navy but once your major service ended what was it like?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: I was concerned about a job on the outside of civilian life. I studied for it and went to work for an insurance company and then took a state examination. Sat for two days and it was pressure vessel engine inspection. I passed the test the first time through. As I remember, eight of us took the test and three of us passed it. Couple of the guys there were sitting there for the third time and still didn't pass it. I'd go out and the insurance company would insure these pieces of machinery and boilers and it was my job to inspect them for safety. If I approved them, I'd write them a permit to operate that piece of machinery. If not, I would not issue a permit and they'd have to repair that piece of machinery before I'd issue a permit.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Besides doing that what else did you do in later years?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well, I went to work for a waterfront for National Steel and Ship Building as a quality and insurance inspector, checking to see if the work was done properly and if the proper materials were used. Then I was promoted to estimator, repair estimator. It was my job to estimate the cost of a job. All machinery items crossed my desk, reduction gears, pumps, blowers, refrigeration, anything engineering. I was there for 11 years.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: And after that anything exciting?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Then I quite and retired in January 1984.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Did you attend any reunions with your shipmates?

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: And how were those like?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: A lot of fun seeing the old shipmates.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What did you guys talk about?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: We kind of reminisced some of the things that went on, where we were at, Iwo Jima, Okinawa, life aboard ship, just things like that.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Can you give me a story you would talk about or anything neat?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well, on the USS Hinsdale, APA-120, which I was on and I was the chief engineer of the boat group in charge of the engineers in each boat. We had twenty-seven boats and I had an engineer on each boat. There was a coxswain and bow hook and it was my job to keep these engines running, fueled and what not. We got ready and made the first landing and the first wave into Okinawa and these boys went in and did their job and came out and the days that they were their we did not lose one boat.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: How did your service experience effect your life?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: It taught me to take orders when I was a youngster in there and then as I moved up the ladder you were the leader of all other people that you worked with in engineering. The controlling in charge of men.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: It was the fact that you had the responsibility for other people's well being and life.

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: As you move up the ladder you accumulate more responsibility.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Oh, I read you were on a ship that a kamikaze crashed into. Can you describe what that was like and what happened during that time?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: That was the Hinsdale. It happened on April 1st which is April Fool's Day but that was the first thing in the morning at daybreak. They hadn't even sounded the general quarters. Every morning a few minutes before sun-up they would sound general quarters for the ship's crew, "man your battle station". I was on the way to a battle station but a guy stopped me and I went into a bake shop and he said a bearing was no good on one of the dough mixers and that's where 10 I was at when the Kamikaze came into a hull right underneath me and went into the fire room and hit a boiler. Everyone in there was killed but one kid. That was it, we were a dead ship. They had to tow us onto the bone yard.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Where in the sea were you at when this happened?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Right one deck above it in the bake shop, the hole in the side of the ship was right below it.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Where in the ocean were you at?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Off of Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: How many were killed exactly?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Thirty-two if I'm not mistaken. 1,500 marines on board at the time. We didn't sink but they towed us in the bone yard where all the crippled ships were. They welded a patch over the hole and pumped the saltwater out. The crew on the repair ship went to work and flushed everything out. They got the engines running again and the pumps and one of the blowers was re-rigged and we steamed home ourselves. One boat, one compressor, one engine. We came back and went to the Panama Canal and New Jersey and they repaired the ship. While we were there it was VE-Day and the war was over.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: So this was all later after you had taken over the ships.

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: That was all back in 43'. This was all in April 45'.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Tell me your most memorable experiences.

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: On the Hinsdale when the Kamikaze hit. 11

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: When you captured the Gough ship it was a history changing moment but it wasn't anything too dramatic because they handed the ship over without hesitation.

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: You were never prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, never was any of our crew on any ship I was on, none. However on the USS Comstock, Huey Long was picked up in Corregidor when he was just a young kid, a fireman. He served over three years as a prisoner of war. Japan had him all during the war and afterwards he came aboard our ship and he knew nothing about engineering. Though, they gave him a rate of CPO but he knew nothing but they gave him a hat and they took care of him.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: You became friends with him then?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Yeah. He didn't talk a lot about what happened to him those three years.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Did you ever win any medals?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: The Atlantic fleet and the Pacific fleet and there was a couple other I forget what they are.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Were those from dedication of service or how were they rewarded?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: I got them because I was on board ships in the Atlantic and I was on board ships in the Pacific in the war area and that was it.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Did you ever get any medals regarding the Gough ship capture?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No I did not. On the Goldsborough we went up to Reykjavik, Iceland with a 12 couple of PBY's and we were servicing them while we were there. The German battleship, Bismarck, had left the fjord in Norway north of Iceland over off of Greenland and back below Iceland. Just before it got off an island off the country of France, the British navy and an American PBY laid a torpedo and knocked its rudder out and the British moved in and sunk it and lost all men, but three. That was exciting when that was going on, it didn't happen in a day, it happened over a period of time.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Did you say you were a part of that?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Our sea planes went out patrolling to try to find it but lost it a couple of times in Iceland and south of Iceland. The planes flying in and out were like a bunch of bumble bees flying in and out of Iceland out the air station looking

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: You found it eventually?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: They found it and took care of it.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: How did they take care of it?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: With guns, they shot it.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Anymore details about the Gough ship?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: The USS Hinsdale, go look on the back of the Times magazine article with Captain Drew.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Any more details on the capture of the Gough ship?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Not really. I can describe Gough. He was just a little man about 5' tall, 13 he ran the whole outfit.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: He was aboard the ship when you obviously captured it?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: [From article] The headman was Gough, an ex rum run-runner supposedly turned respectful, who pulled much of his information from a lousy Cologne night club besides getting servicemen and cannel employees to buy them drinks of colored water at .75 a drink. The cabaret girls were paid off for information they picked up on shipmates. Girls got information of naval labor sent to Panama through an agency his brother helped to run as part of the Gough Brothers Enterprises. Probably more was a fleet often small schooners that used to reveal Nazi subs at clandestine rendezvous.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: So you land your plane, you get onto the ship, you pack down the doors, your crew splits off. Half go to the control room. How many go to the engine room?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Just two of us.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: How many in the engine room?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: One

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Were they surprised?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Of course.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: They were totally in shock and surrendered without any problem?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: What happened once you captured them and they were sent off as prisoners of war? What happened to the ship captured and oil on the ship? 14

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Oil was checked in and unloaded and it was carrying quite a large load of bale of cloth like bales of hay. These were rows of bale of cloth and possibly armory or artillery submarine head or what not and they might be hidden in one of those bales and so we had stevedores come aboard and roll one bale at a time instead of breaking it open. Having all the bales of cloth strung around we took a magnetic compass and carried it around the bale to see if there was any metal or iron in there. Then we went down and checked for hidden compartments and if there were any compartments hanging under the ship we threw a line over the bow and seesawed all the way back to the stern to see if there was anything under the ship. Then we turned it over to the British authorities.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Were you ever thanked for doing that?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, just part of over job.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: So this is later on, now today did your military experience influence your thinking about the war or military in general?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well, we had no newspapers, no radios or private radios we could listen to. There was no communication or news that would tell us how the war was going, what was going on.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: It was the seclusion that you did not like about being on a ship?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: It didn't enter my mind, it was part of my job. As soon as they left port, the radios were dead because it was outside of radio communication. We were not informed of anything that was going on.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Did you mind?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Sure, we were kept uninformed. 15

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Once you did find out what did happen what were your views of the war?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: I happened to be on times square VE-day when Europe folded. Our ship was at Hoboken N.J. and three of us were in NY across the river in Times Square. VE- day I was there with thousands and thousands of people, it was very exciting.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: And now we have the war in Iraq, how is your views now? Did your service change the way you view war or did it change your way of why wars were fought?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, not once.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: You could have not served a day and you'd have the same view?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Right. The crew was just doing our job, they allowed us liberty to just go ashore. There were no towns around, no natives, so we had this harbor to ourselves. So we went swimming with the seals and amphibious dragons. This was where Darwin was in Galapagos Islands. It was very exciting.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Were there any other memories like that that stick in your mind?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well, that was one of them. Saint Lucia, when we were anchored there we could see the bottom thirty feet down the water was so clear. One of the crewmembers caught a fifteen-foot shark and he hauled it up, put it on a block and tackle. He cut out the jaws and he wanted the teeth and I got the two eyeballs. I cut the lens out of the eyeballs and cured them and anyways they were stolen from me later. People made ring sets or brooches out of them. Anyway, I got a couple of the teeth and you can wet your hair on your arm and you can shave it off with a sharks tooth. 16

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: You taught me one time that backgammon game.

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: We played that all the time.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Any other games like that that you played to entertain yourself?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, it was primarily backgammon. Some of the guys played poker or shot crabs which was still legal and if they caught them they'd take the money. But that acey ducey, that backgammon game, is played similar but different.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: On the ships did you ever engage in ship to ship combat?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No, because we were an EPA, we weren't a combat ship, we carried the troops. We were a personnel carrier. We had guns on board but we didn't go out with a company of ships looking for the enemy. They protected us. We were always in convoy because we were carrying the troops.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: How many were aboard on your ship?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Well at different times 1200, 1500, marines.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: How many ships did you sail on?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: Texas, Wyoming, Fairfax, Go Ids borough, PC 791, Hinsdale, Platte, Chemund, and Mathews. During the Korean War, I was on a USS Hector, a repair ship, we made the landing, the Inchon landing where they put the troops a shore in Korea. Later, I came back and was in a machinist school in the Great Lakes. I was an instructor there. After that tour of duty, I went back to the Pacific coast and was on a fleet oilier where we would fuel ships under way with an aircraft carrier on one side and a cruiser or destroyer on the other. I forget where they were bombarding Korea [?] and the ships would fuel up and go in and 17 bombard. There would be another right behind him come along side and as soon as we are out of fuel we'd go down to refuel the ship and go back up and take care of it the second time.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Anything else you'd like to add?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: That pretty much sums it up. Oh, one more. During the war, the USS Hinsdale, the last trip I was on, we went up to Seattle and every year the Navy with one of them like the Mathews had to go up to the Dribloph Islands north of the Bering Seas, north of the Aleutian Islands and had to pick up seal's skin and blubber. We worked there for one week, loading that stuff for the natives up there. Male seals were killed for pelts and blubber. On the last day the captain came down and wanted a boat and a couple of guys to go fishing with him. So we took a boat and went out fishing for.... anyway we caught a sixty-pound fish and pulling a sixty-pound fish up from the bottom. Oh that's delicious, right from the ocean into the frying pan and on your plate. Fresh fish, albacore! No it wasn't albacore; it was a different fish [?] I don't know. On the Golsborough, we ran into heavy seas, we always traveled alone. We were never in convoy with other ships. Anyways, we hit rough seas and the swallows were at least twenty to forty feet high. We lost one of the kids over the side in the North Atlantic. Kid by the name of Willet from Nantucket, Rhode Island. The captain had the ship turn around and go down below. They threw a life jacket out [?] There is a battery that comes on, a flashlight, as soon as it hits salt water. The life ring landed near him so the captain had the ship turn around and go back and then turn around again and come up on him. They saw the life ring but they didn't see anyone hanging on it. Now to get back to when he was turning because of the swells so high, we rolled sixty-three degrees. So the ship was almost laying on it's side. So that's how far over [?] And an officer who was on the bridge checked chronometer and it was sixty -three degrees. Why we didn't capsize and keep rolling is just one of those things.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Other than that you didn't witness much death or anything memory provoking?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: No not really.

sp.speaker: Kristina Kalchev
sp.p: Anything else you'd like to add?

sp.speaker: John Bellock
sp.p: That's about it.
